attempts.hypothesis: Contact is fatal and sensing is untrustworthy, so I'm building a conservative reactive navigator that fuses GPS+compass, chooses steering by a corridor-clearance (VFH-style) score over a persistent obstacle map (covers blind/missing rays), and escapes stalls/pockets by reversing and boundary-followi

Contact is fatal and sensing is untrustworthy, so I'm using a conservative reactive navigator that fuses GPS+compass heading correction, boundary and corridor-centred obstacle avoidance with emergency overrides, and a backup-and-turn recovery loop with cooldowns.

The compass has a large bias and sensors can momentarily miss obstacles, so I estimate heading from compass-rate integration with GPS-velocity correction, guard against dropouts with persistent ray minimums, use gentler steering gains to kill the zigzag oscillation, and recover from stalls by spinni

The compass bias drives oscillatory steering loops, so I navigate via the cross-product of GPS velocity and target direction (robust to compass errors) with rate-limited steering smoothing and alternating stall recovery.

Speed was gated only by forward clearance which ignored dangerously close side walls, so I now throttle by the minimum of all five rays, add symmetric side-avoidance steering, PD control with heading-rate damping, and GPS-velocity heading estimation to handle compass bias.

The compass has a ~20° clockwise bias and sensors briefly miss obstacles, so I'm using GPS-velocity heading with online compass-bias learning, aggressive unscaled steering toward the target, persistent ray minimums for safety, and recovery that reverse-spins with fast-decay gap-finding before re-eng

I believe local range sensing is best handled by cautious target pursuit with persistent wall following, so this attempt adds speed-aware braking, clearance steering, GPS heading correction, and escape turns.

The first controller over-steered and oscillated near obstacles, so this version uses smoothed pursuit, latched bug-style obstacle bypassing, conservative clearance and braking, boundary repulsion, and timed dead-end escapes.

I believe the previous run was dominated by high-gain command reversals and a rover trapped without a decisive recovery, so this version uses slew-limited steering, persistent clearance-based wall bypassing, and a bounded reverse/U-turn escape.

I believe persistent low-gain bug-style wall following is safer than reactive steering, so this version latches a bypass side, limits turning and acceleration, and uses decisive alternate-side escapes for dead ends.
The previous run was dominated by delayed high-gain heading oscillation, so this version uses rate-damped low-differential pursuit with latched clearance following and measured U-turn recovery.

I believe the main failure is low-power recovery inside pockets, so this version keeps latched wall routing but uses faster sensor recovery, speed-based stall detection, and a decisive timed reverse/U-turn escape.

I believe the earlier runs were trapped by premature wall-route exits and an over-rotating fixed recovery turn, so this version holds bug routes longer, learns small heading bias, and uses feedback-braked alternate-side escapes.

I believe the previous runs over-rotated into pockets, so this controller uses slower damped pursuit, clearance-aware latched wall routing with dynamic side changes, and short feedback-driven escapes.
I believe safe progress depends on reacting early to narrow clearances, so this controller seeks the next target while slowing near obstacles and steering toward the more open side.
The first run shows that steering and avoidance are too aggressive and oscillatory, so I’m smoothing turns, slowing earlier near obstacles, and committing briefly to the clearer side.
The trace suggests steering inertia is causing repeated overshoot, so I’m adding yaw-rate damping, earlier speed-based braking, and more persistent obstacle avoidance.
The rover appears to react too late and become trapped when its route is blocked, so I’m slowing earlier, steering around remembered ray hits, and backing out when progress stalls.

The fourth run became trapped in a steering and reverse loop at a barrier, so I’m adding a coarse remembered A* route, steadier forward obstacle avoidance, and a brief turn-and-go recovery when progress stalls.
Repeated runs stop at the same obstruction, so I’m replacing the brittle global detour with ray-based heading selection, a committed bypass side, and breadcrumb backtracking for dead ends.
The rover seems to get trapped by reversing and unstable detours, so I’m using forward-biased clearance steering, committing briefly to an open side, and switching sides if progress stalls.

The repeated stalls look like local steering loops rather than just excess speed, so I’m adding a rolling ray-hit map and grid route planner with conservative local avoidance and a side-step recovery.

I will use a conservative adaptive reactive controller that estimates compass bias from GPS motion, tracks the target bearing, and blends ray-based obstacle avoidance with stuck recovery, since the physics and sensor errors are unknown.

I think the last run failed mainly from reacting too late and too sharply to front rocks, so I am keeping target tracking but adding earlier obstacle override, lower-gain smoothed steering, and conservative speed control to handle apparent actuator lag.

I think the main failure was getting trapped in local rock pockets, so I am adding a coarse occupancy-grid A* planner from ray hits plus a commit-based escape recovery, while keeping target tracking and compass-bias estimation.

The previous attempt suffered from heavy A* causing an interruption, so I am switching to a lightweight coarse-grid A* with a strict expansion limit and a strong reactive fallback, while keeping compass-bias estimation and robust stuck recovery.

The A* planner caused execution interruptions, so I am replacing it with a lightweight reactive state machine (target, turn, wall) that uses ray-based obstacle avoidance and wall-following for dead ends, plus the same compass bias and stuck recovery.

I am replacing the oscillation-prone reactive state machine with a lightweight gap-scoring controller that commits to an avoidance mode until the target direction is actually clear, while keeping gentle steering/hysteresis and the compass-bias estimate.

The world appears to have significant compass bias and local minima from rocks, so I am adding a lightweight persistent occupancy-grid A* planner with conservative ray-based safety and bias estimation.

I am keeping the lightweight A* mapper but making heading estimation and calibration more robust, using pure-pursuit path following with softer reactive avoidance, and adding an emergency back-off so the rover does not stall or crash in narrow rock pockets.
